options.A: It eliminates the need for routine hand hygiene protocols
options.B: It helps distinguish normal endemic levels from emerging outbreaks
options.C: It determines the financial budget for laboratory equipment
options.D: It guarantees complete eradication of hospital-acquired infections

explanation: Knowing the usual baseline allows staff to immediately spot unusual spikes or clusters that signal a developing public health threat. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary objective of public health surveillance?

options.A: Providing free medications to all citizens
options.B: Managing hospital human resource departments
options.C: Providing timely information for health action
options.D: Conducting clinical drug trials for pharmaceutical firms

explanation: The core goal of surveillance is to gather data that drives prompt public health decisions and interventions. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h2)

question: How do surveillance data directly support national policymakers?

options.A: By regulating the retail pricing of imported surgical supplies
options.B: By determining the architectural design of community clinics
options.C: By setting individual nursing shift rosters in regional hospitals
options.D: By guiding the deployment of immunization campaigns and response teams

explanation: Accurate tracking data informs leaders where resources and interventions are most urgently needed during health crises. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h2)

question: Which surveillance type relies on health workers voluntarily submitting reports of diagnosed cases?

options.A: Passive surveillance
options.B: Laboratory-based surveillance
options.C: Active surveillance
options.D: Sentinel surveillance

explanation: Passive surveillance waits for reports to be sent in by clinicians, making it inexpensive but prone to missed cases. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h3)

question: What is the main characteristic of sentinel surveillance?

options.A: Checking every single patient admitted to national hospitals
options.B: Using a select network of sites to monitor general trends
options.C: Waiting for patients to report symptoms without laboratory tests
options.D: Focusing exclusively on environmental water and soil samples

explanation: Sentinel systems use designated high-quality reporting sites to represent broader epidemiological patterns efficiently. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of using standardized case definitions in surveillance?

options.A: Ensuring uniform classification of cases across different locations
options.B: Reducing the financial cost of purchasing laboratory reagents
options.C: Speeding up the discharge process for hospitalized patients
options.D: Eliminating the need for patient consent during data collection

explanation: Standard definitions ensure that everyone counts the same clinical picture as a case, making data comparable across regions. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h4)

question: A clinic in a remote area lacks computers but maintains accurate admission and laboratory registers. How do these paper registers serve surveillance?

options.A: They prevent the emergence of new microbial strains
options.B: They act as foundational tools for capturing basic health data
options.C: They automatically transmit digital alerts to the ministry
options.D: They replace the need for national public health policies

explanation: Manual registers are vital baseline records from which data can be manually collated and reported upward in settings lacking digital infrastructure. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h4)

question: Why are bedside nurses considered vital to microbial surveillance?

options.A: They are typically the first to notice unusual symptom clusters or infection spikes
options.B: They hold exclusive authority to declare national epidemic states
options.C: They manufacture all diagnostic test kits used in public hospitals
options.D: They manage the federal health budget for infectious disease control

explanation: Direct and continuous patient contact puts nurses in the best position to spot early signs of emerging infections or outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h5)

question: A ward nurse notices that three patients in the same bay developed sudden surgical site purulent discharge within forty-eight hours. What immediate nursing action supports surveillance?

options.A: Prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics without consulting the medical team
options.B: Discharging all three patients immediately to prevent cross-contamination
options.C: Waiting until the end of the month to include the cases in routine audits
options.D: Documenting the findings and reporting the cluster to the infection control team

explanation: Prompt reporting of clinical clusters allows surveillance systems to investigate and contain potential hospital-acquired outbreaks early. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h5)

question: What is the initial step typically taken when surveillance data signals a potential outbreak?

options.A: Verifying the diagnosis and confirming the outbreak
options.B: Holding a press conference to announce a national disaster
options.C: Closing all healthcare facilities in the affected region
options.D: Destroying all historical laboratory records from the unit

explanation: Before launching a full investigation, health teams must verify that reported cases represent a true outbreak rather than a data artifact or diagnostic error. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h6)

question: Why is descriptive epidemiology (time, place, person analysis) crucial during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: It calculates the exact financial cost of treating every patient
options.B: It helps characterize the spread and identify likely sources of transmission
options.C: It determines the individual nurse's liability for the infection
options.D: It replaces the need for laboratory confirmation of the pathogen

explanation: Analyzing who is getting sick, where they are, and when symptoms started points investigators toward the source of the outbreak. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge for surveillance in developing healthcare systems?

options.A: Severe workforce shortages of trained public health staff
options.B: Delays in data transmission caused by poor connectivity
options.C: Excessive surplus of advanced diagnostic testing laboratories
options.D: Erratic power supply compromising cold-chain specimen storage

explanation: Developing systems typically suffer from a scarcity, not a surplus, of advanced diagnostic facilities. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h7)

question: How do workforce shortages impact routine surveillance activities in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Data accuracy improves because fewer people handle the records
options.B: Paper registers are instantly replaced by fully automated digital systems
options.C: Staff members automatically receive higher salaries to compensate
options.D: Surveillance tasks become an overburdened add-on, leading to delayed reporting

explanation: When clinical staff are overwhelmed with direct patient care, surveillance reporting often gets delayed or neglected. [learn more](GST114_U2_T15#GST114_U2_T15_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of placing individuals in quarantine?

options.A: To provide permanent shelter for chronically ill patients
options.B: To separate healthy exposed persons to prevent disease spread
options.C: To treat active symptoms of a diagnosed infection
options.D: To conduct terminal disinfection of contaminated personal items

explanation: Quarantine is specifically applied to individuals who are currently well but have had exposure to a contagious pathogen, keeping them away from the general public until the incubation period passes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h1)

question: How is the duration of a quarantine period scientifically determined?

options.A: By the administrative schedule set by local municipal authorities
options.B: By the total number of hospital beds available in the region
options.C: By the average recovery time of patients admitted to the intensive care unit
options.D: By the longest known incubation period of the specific infectious agent

explanation: The timeline for restricting movement is strictly dictated by how long the pathogen takes to manifest symptoms after initial exposure. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h1)

question: Which population is targeted by isolation protocols?

options.A: Individuals who are confirmed to be infected with a contagious disease
options.B: Community members living near an outbreak zone with no known contact
options.C: Healthcare workers who have completed their shift in a high-risk ward
options.D: Healthy travelers arriving from countries with low immunization rates

explanation: Isolation separates individuals who are already sick and infectious from those who are healthy to stop active transmission chains. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h2)

question: A patient with laboratory-confirmed Lassa fever is placed in a negative pressure room. This intervention is best described as what?

options.A: Quarantine because it involves a dangerous viral pathogen
options.B: Prophylaxis because it prevents secondary complications
options.C: Social distancing because it limits visitors to the ward
options.D: Isolation because the patient has an active, confirmed infection

explanation: Because the patient is actively sick with a confirmed disease, separating them from others constitutes isolation rather than quarantine. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h2)

question: What defines the incubation period of an infectious disease?

options.A: The total duration a patient remains contagious after full recovery
options.B: The timeframe required for antibiotic therapy to eradicate a virus
options.C: The time between pathogen exposure and the onset of clinical symptoms
options.D: The speed at which a bacterium multiplies on artificial agar plates

explanation: The incubation period represents the silent phase before clinical manifestations emerge, which is the exact window quarantine targets. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h3)

question: Why can an exposed individual transmit an infection during quarantine despite having no symptoms?

options.A: Asymptomatic carriers never develop antibodies against the disease
options.B: They may be shedding the infectious agent during the incubation window
options.C: Environmental toxins mimic the pathogen and trigger false positives
options.D: Their immune system is actively destroying the pathogen too quickly

explanation: Many contagious agents replicate and shed before clinical signs appear, making asymptomatic transmission a primary threat managed by quarantine. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h3)

question: What characterizes facility-based quarantine compared to home quarantine?

options.A: It utilizes centralized government-designated locations for groups
options.B: It allows unrestricted movement within public market areas
options.C: It is reserved exclusively for patients with severe acute respiratory failure
options.D: It is managed by individuals inside their own private apartments

explanation: Facility-based quarantine houses exposed individuals in managed centralized spaces rather than their private homes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h4)

question: When is compulsory quarantine legally invoked by public health authorities?

options.A: When voluntary compliance by exposed individuals fails or is deemed unreliable
options.B: During the annual clearance of hospital pharmaceutical inventory
options.C: As a routine requirement for all newly hired nursing staff
options.D: Whenever a single routine vaccination appointment is missed

explanation: Compulsory measures are legal mandates used when voluntary adherence is insufficient to protect public health and safety. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h4)

question: Which of the following is a primary public health trigger for instituting quarantine?

options.A: An outbreak of a novel, highly contagious pathogen with pandemic potential
options.B: A seasonal increase in uncomplicated iron-deficiency anemia
options.C: The routine quarterly maintenance of municipal water purification plants
options.D: An isolated case of chronic degenerative joint disease

explanation: Quarantine is deployed for serious, contagious threats that possess the capacity to rapidly overwhelm healthcare systems and spread widely. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h5)

question: What factor do public health officials prioritize when deciding whether to enforce population quarantine?

options.A: The aesthetic appeal of the designated housing facilities
options.B: The transmission mode and severity of the infectious agent
options.C: The personal travel preferences of the exposed individuals
options.D: The market price of commercial cleaning supplies

explanation: Officials weigh how easily a pathogen spreads and how severe the resulting disease is to justify restricting movement. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h5)

question: Which federal agency plays a central role in coordinating public health responses and disease containment in Nigeria?

options.A: Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC)
options.B: National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)
options.C: Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC)
options.D: Standard Organisation of Nigeria (SON)

explanation: The NCDC is the national public health institute tasked with leading disease surveillance, preparedness, and outbreak response across Nigeria. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h6)

question: What ethical principle justifies the enforcement of quarantine during a severe disease outbreak?

options.A: Beneficence and the protection of collective community safety
options.B: Elimination of all documentation requirements for travelers
options.C: Complete individual autonomy regardless of public risk
options.D: Financial profit optimization for local health facilities

explanation: Ethical frameworks justify restricting individual movement when necessary to protect the wider population from catastrophic harm. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h6)

question: What is a core clinical responsibility of a nurse monitoring individuals in quarantine?

options.A: Administering terminal surgical procedures for chronic conditions
options.B: Conducting forensic autopsies on deceased community members
options.C: Issuing international passports and travel visas
options.D: Performing daily symptom screenings and temperature checks

explanation: Regular physiological tracking allows nurses to detect the earliest indicators of infection during the incubation period. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h7)

question: Why must nurses evaluate the psychological well-being of individuals undergoing quarantine?

options.A: Depression automatically grants immunity against viral pathogens
options.B: Mental instability prevents the human body from producing white blood cells
options.C: Psychological evaluations replace the need for physical temperature logging
options.D: Confinement frequently triggers anxiety, frustration, and emotional distress

explanation: Isolation and restricted movement take a heavy psychological toll, requiring nurses to monitor and support mental health during confinement. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h7)

question: Which action is critical to prevent a quarantine facility from amplifying disease transmission?

options.A: Strict adherence to infection prevention and control protocols
options.B: Storing biomedical waste in open corridors for easy access
options.C: Eliminating all handwashing stations to conserve water supplies
options.D: Permitting unrestricted daily visits from community members

explanation: Rigorous IPC measures, including PPE use and waste management, ensure that the containment site itself does not spread the infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of establishing clear spatial zoning within a quarantine facility?

options.A: To simplify the architectural design blueprints for construction engineers
options.B: To ensure that administrative staff have larger bedrooms than quarantined guests
options.C: To separate clean administrative areas from contaminated zones and prevent cross-contamination
options.D: To reduce the overall electricity consumption of the facility

explanation: Zoning creates physical boundaries that protect healthcare workers and clean areas from exposure to infectious pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h8)

question: What is an immediate consequence of failing to provide adequate psychosocial and informational support during quarantine?

options.A: Automatic extension of the incubation period for all pathogens
options.B: Increased risk of resistance, anxiety, and breaches of containment
options.C: Accelerated physical healing and improved metabolic function
options.D: Immediate eradication of the infectious agent from the environment

explanation: Without clear communication and emotional backing, individuals often experience high anxiety and may attempt to leave quarantine prematurely. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h9)

question: Which nursing intervention best fosters compliance among individuals confined to a quarantine facility?

options.A: Providing clear education, reliable communication channels, and meeting basic physical needs
options.B: Isolating residents completely from any form of news or external contact
options.C: Restricting food and water intake to encourage faster symptom resolution
options.D: Refusing to answer questions regarding the expected duration of confinement

explanation: Trust is built when nurses address physical needs, answer questions transparently, and maintain open lines of communication. [learn more](GST114_U2_T16#GST114_U2_T16_h9)

question: What is the primary purpose of isolation in a healthcare setting?

options.A: To interrupt the transmission of pathogenic microorganisms
options.B: To completely eliminate all bacteria from the hospital ward
options.C: To punish patients who fail to comply with hygiene rules
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of treating chronic illnesses

explanation: Separating infected patients physically restricts the spread of pathogens to susceptible individuals within the facility. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h1)

question: Why are immunocompromised patients particularly targeted for protection through isolation protocols?

options.A: They always harbor airborne multidrug-resistant organisms
options.B: Their natural defense mechanisms are weakened, making them prone to severe infections
options.C: Their metabolic rate prevents standard medications from working effectively
options.D: They require higher doses of intravenous antibiotics than other patients

explanation: Patients with depressed immunity cannot easily fight off opportunistic microbes picked up from the hospital environment. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h1)

question: Which link in the chain of infection is primarily targeted when implementing barrier isolation precautions?

options.A: Patient genetic susceptibility
options.B: Infectious agent mutation rate
options.C: Mode of transmission
options.D: Original reservoir source

explanation: Barriers like gloves, gowns, and masks directly block the pathway pathogens use to travel from the source to a new host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h2)

question: A patient coughs and expels droplets containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis into the air. What link in the chain of infection does the cough represent?

options.A: Infectious reservoir
options.B: Susceptible host
options.C: Infectious agent
options.D: Portal of exit

explanation: The respiratory tract acts as the route through which the pathogen leaves the infected individual's body. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h2)

question: To which group of patients do standard precautions apply?

options.A: Individuals showing active symptoms of respiratory illness
options.B: All patients regardless of their diagnosis or infection status
options.C: Only patients confirmed to have a bloodborne pathogen
options.D: Patients admitted exclusively to intensive care units

explanation: Standard precautions form the baseline level of infection control for every single patient interaction in healthcare. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h3)

question: What is the primary rationale for applying standard precautions universally rather than selectively?

options.A: Laboratory test results are always available immediately upon admission
options.B: Many infected individuals may be asymptomatic or undiagnosed
options.C: Hospital accreditation agencies require universal charting for all supplies
options.D: It eliminates the need for handwashing between different patients

explanation: Because infectious status is not always known, treating all bodily fluids with caution prevents accidental exposure. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h3)

question: Which type of room ventilation is required for a patient placed on airborne precautions?

options.A: Naturally ventilated open ward
options.B: Negative pressure room
options.C: Positive pressure room
options.D: Standard laminar flow

explanation: Negative pressure keeps air from flowing out into the hallway when the door is opened, trapping airborne droplet nuclei inside. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h4)

question: A patient is admitted with a confirmed diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis. Which specific barrier protection must the nurse wear when entering this room?

options.A: Face shield without a mask
options.B: N95 respirator
options.C: Standard surgical mask
options.D: Clean non-sterile gloves only

explanation: Tuberculosis spreads via airborne droplet nuclei, necessitating a fitted respirator that filters out tiny suspended particles. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h4)

question: According to standard protocol, which item of personal protective equipment is typically removed first during doffing?

options.A: Mask
options.B: Goggles
options.C: Gloves
options.D: Gown

explanation: Gloves are considered the most contaminated item and are removed first to prevent transferring pathogens to other parts of the body or clothing. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h5)

question: Why is performing hand hygiene immediately after removing personal protective equipment critical?

options.A: Microorganisms may have transferred to the hands during the removal process
options.B: Soap activates the residual chemicals left behind on discarded gowns
options.C: It cools down the skin after wearing non-breathable plastic gloves
options.D: Hospital policy mandates tracking hand hygiene frequency per shift

explanation: Even with careful technique, accidental contact with outer surfaces of PPE can contaminate the hands during doffing. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h5)

question: What should be done with diagnostic equipment like stethoscopes used on a patient in strict isolation?

options.A: Share them freely across all beds in the general ward
options.B: Wipe them with water and return them to the central station
options.C: Keep them dedicated inside the patient's room
options.D: Submerge them in boiling water after every single use

explanation: Using dedicated equipment prevents the inadvertent mechanical transfer of pathogens to non-isolated patients. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h6)

question: Why must soiled linen from an isolation room be handled with minimal agitation?

options.A: To prevent aerosolizing infectious pathogens into the surrounding air
options.B: To ensure the fabric color does not fade during chemical processing
options.C: To reduce the electrical power consumed by hospital laundry services
options.D: To keep the laundry from tearing before reaching the washing machine

explanation: Shaking or tossing contaminated linen disperses dust and microbes into the atmosphere, creating an inhalation hazard. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h6)

question: Which psychological response is most commonly observed in patients placed under prolonged isolation?

options.A: Complete memory loss of the admission event
options.B: Aggressive hostility toward medical staff
options.C: Depression and feelings of loneliness
options.D: Euphoria and uncharacteristic excitement

explanation: Sensory deprivation and separation from social support networks frequently trigger depressive symptoms in isolated patients. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h7)

question: What is NOT a recommended nursing strategy for mitigating the psychosocial impact of isolation?

options.A: Scheduling regular check-ins to address patient fears and concerns
options.B: Limiting all verbal communication to prevent staff contamination
options.C: Explaining the clinical reasons behind the isolation precautions clearly
options.D: Facilitating video calls between the patient and their family members

explanation: Cutting off verbal interaction increases feelings of abandonment; nurses should communicate regularly while wearing appropriate barriers. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h7)

question: Whose primary responsibility is it to monitor and enforce visitor compliance with isolation guidelines on a hospital ward?

options.A: The hospital security guard
options.B: The visiting family members
options.C: The facility finance officer
options.D: The attending nurse

explanation: Nurses coordinate direct patient care environments and actively educate and monitor visitors regarding proper PPE usage. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h8)

question: Why is accurate charting of isolation protocols by the nurse critical for the wider healthcare facility?

options.A: It replaces the need for verbal shift handovers at the nursing station
options.B: It proves to patients that their room charges are fully justified
options.C: It ensures continuity of care and alerts all multidisciplinary team members to safety requirements
options.D: It calculates the exact financial bonus due to the nursing staff each month

explanation: Clear documentation informs every incoming clinician and support worker about necessary barrier precautions before room entry. [learn more](GST114_U2_T17#GST114_U2_T17_h8)

question: What is the primary public health goal of contact tracing during an infectious disease outbreak?

options.A: To enforce legal penalties on individuals who fail to report symptoms
options.B: To conduct mass vaccination campaigns across urban populations
options.C: To replace hospital-based care with community-managed isolation
options.D: To break transmission chains by locating and managing exposed individuals

explanation: Contact tracing focuses on finding people exposed to an infected person so they can be monitored and managed before spreading the disease further. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h1)

question: Why does contact tracing represent a shift from passive to active healthcare management?

options.A: It brings health workers into the community to find cases rather than waiting for sick people to arrive at hospitals
options.B: It eliminates the need for laboratory diagnostic confirmation during outbreaks
options.C: It transfers clinical decision-making authority entirely from doctors to community leaders
options.D: It relies on automated digital tracking systems instead of human interaction

explanation: Active surveillance involves health personnel proactively seeking out potential cases in the community instead of waiting passively for patients to present at clinics. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h1)

question: Which link in the chain of infection is directly targeted and interrupted by contact tracing?

options.A: Mode of transmission
options.B: Infectious agent
options.C: Reservoir
options.D: Portal of entry

explanation: By identifying and separating exposed individuals before they become infectious, contact tracing stops the pathogen from transmitting to a new host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h2)

question: What role does the incubation period play in planning a contact tracing protocol?

options.A: It calculates the total number of hospital beds needed during a surge
options.B: It determines the duration for which identified contacts must be monitored or quarantined
options.C: It establishes the geographical boundaries of the affected community
options.D: It identifies the exact laboratory test required to confirm the pathogen

explanation: The incubation period dictates the maximum time window a person might develop symptoms, which defines how long they need active monitoring. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h2)

question: Which criterion typically defines a high-risk or close contact during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: Face-to-face interaction within one meter for more than 15 minutes
options.B: Residing in the same municipal local government area as the case
options.C: Passing by the infected person briefly in an open outdoor corridor
options.D: Working in the same large multi-story commercial building

explanation: Close contact definitions generally rely on physical proximity and duration of exposure, which substantially raise the likelihood of pathogen transmission. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h3)

question: Why is it clinically necessary to categorize contacts into high-risk and low-risk tiers?

options.A: To assign legal liability for the initial transmission event within the community
options.B: To determine whether the index case requires surgical or medical intervention
options.C: To simplify the statistical data entry required for national health bulletins
options.D: To optimize the allocation of limited public health resources toward individuals most likely to develop disease

explanation: Categorization allows health teams to focus intensive monitoring, testing, and quarantine enforcement where the risk of secondary transmission is highest. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h3)

question: What is the most effective approach when interviewing an index case about their daily movements?

options.A: Demanding a written log before beginning any verbal conversation
options.B: Involving local law enforcement officers to compel truthful answers
options.C: Employing a strict interrogative tone to ensure the patient does not lie
options.D: Using a supportive tone with open-ended questions to encourage open recall

explanation: A supportive, non-judgmental approach builds trust and helps patients remember details they might otherwise hide out of fear or stigma. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h4)

question: A patient appears defensive and expresses fear that their employer will find out about their diagnosis. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Reassure the patient regarding strict confidentiality protocols and privacy protections
options.B: Explain that the employer must be notified immediately by law to protect coworkers
options.C: Threaten mandatory institutional quarantine if they refuse to cooperate
options.D: Postpone the interview indefinitely until the patient calms down on their own

explanation: Addressing fears of stigma and reassuring patients about confidentiality is essential to secure their cooperation during contact tracing interviews. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h4)

question: What is the primary operational difference between quarantine and isolation?

options.A: Quarantine is voluntary, whereas isolation requires a court order in every instance
options.B: Quarantine applies only to bacterial infections, while isolation applies only to viral pathogens
options.C: Quarantine restricts exposed individuals who are not yet sick, while isolation separates sick individuals who are infectious
options.D: Quarantine is managed in a hospital setting, while isolation is managed exclusively at home

explanation: Quarantine is for healthy people who had exposure, while isolation is for those who have confirmed or suspected active illness. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h5)

question: Why is providing logistical support such as food and communication credit essential for successful home quarantine?

options.A: It removes the necessity for individuals to leave their homes for basic supplies, ensuring compliance
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will recover from the illness without requiring medication
options.C: It replaces the need for daily temperature checks and symptom reporting
options.D: It fulfills legal requirements mandated by international trade organizations

explanation: People cannot successfully stay home if they lack food or water; supporting their basic needs makes adherence to quarantine feasible. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h5)

question: What is the primary ethical risk of breaching a patient's confidentiality during contact tracing?

options.A: It automatically invalidates all laboratory test results in the affected region
options.B: It destroys community trust, causing people to hide symptoms and avoid public health workers
options.C: It increases the biological mutation rate of the infectious pathogen
options.D: It prevents health workers from accessing essential medical supplies from the government

explanation: When confidentiality is broken, fear of stigma causes individuals to conceal illnesses, which undermines entire disease control efforts. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT an acceptable ethical practice for nurses engaged in contact tracing?

options.A: Explaining the rationale for quarantine clearly before enforcing restrictions
options.B: Disclosing the name of the index case to contacts to convince them of the exposure risk
options.C: Balancing community safety needs with respect for individual autonomy
options.D: Protecting patient health records from unauthorized viewing by coworkers or neighbors

explanation: Nurses must never reveal the identity of the index case; contacts can be warned of exposure without knowing who infected them. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h6)

question: What is a primary logistical challenge to contact tracing in many urban Nigerian settings?

options.A: Excessive availability of private vehicle transport for all residents
options.B: Imprecise residential addresses and high population mobility
options.C: A complete absence of mobile telecommunication networks
options.D: Mandatory international travel restrictions between states

explanation: In many dense areas, lack of formal street naming and frequent movement make physically locating contacts difficult. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h7)

question: Why is collaborating with local leaders and traditional rulers essential for successful outbreak control in Nigeria?

options.A: They hold community trust and help reduce suspicion and resistance against health workers
options.B: They are legally mandated to replace government nurses during a crisis
options.C: They manage the financial budget for international health organizations
options.D: They possess formal medical degrees required to diagnose infectious diseases

explanation: Involving respected community figures bridges the gap between public health teams and local residents, securing cooperation and dispelling rumors. [learn more](GST114_U2_T18#GST114_U2_T18_h7)

question: What direction of inquiry best describes a case-control study?

options.A: Prospective inquiry moving from cause to effect
options.B: Experimental inquiry manipulating the exposure status
options.C: Retrospective inquiry moving from effect to cause
options.D: Cross-sectional inquiry measuring exposure and outcome simultaneously

explanation: Case-control studies begin with individuals who already have the disease or outcome and look backward in time to determine their prior exposure history. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h1)

question: Why are case-control designs particularly useful during acute disease outbreaks in resource-limited settings?

options.A: They can be conducted quickly with relatively small sample sizes
options.B: They prove the absolute biological mechanism of pathogen transmission
options.C: They require long-term follow-up of healthy populations
options.D: They completely eliminate all forms of measurement bias

explanation: Because cases are already identified and available, retrospective designs save time and financial resources during public health emergencies. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h1)

question: What primary characteristic must a control group possess in a valid case-control study?

options.A: They must have a higher socioeconomic status than the cases
options.B: They must already show early, subclinical signs of the disease
options.C: They must be completely immune to the infectious agent
options.D: They must come from the same source population as the cases

explanation: Controls must be representative of the population that generated the cases to prevent selection bias from distorting the association. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h2)

question: A researcher selects hospital patients with severe malaria as cases and healthy neighborhood volunteers as controls. What major methodological pitfall does this introduce?

options.A: Reverse causality where the outcome causes the exposure
options.B: Information bias resulting from inaccurate laboratory equipment
options.C: Selection bias due to differing baseline health-seeking behaviors
options.D: Confounding by age and sex in every participant

explanation: Hospital cases and community controls often differ systematically in healthcare access and underlying health status, threatening study validity. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h2)

question: What is the primary danger of recall bias in retrospective exposure assessment?

options.A: Cases remember past exposures differently than healthy controls
options.B: Researchers accidentally reveal group allocations to participants
options.C: Study subjects refuse to participate in hospital interviews
options.D: Laboratory instruments misidentify the causative microorganism

explanation: Individuals suffering from a serious illness often search their memories more intensively for causes, leading to differential reporting compared to healthy controls. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h3)

question: How do researchers best protect against interviewer bias during data collection in a case-control study?

options.A: Providing leading questions to ensure participants remember the exposure
options.B: Conducting interviews only after the data analysis phase is completed
options.C: Allowing interviewers to choose which patients fit the diagnostic criteria
options.D: Using blinded interviewers who do not know whether a participant is a case or a control

explanation: Blinding the personnel collecting data prevents them from subconsciously guiding or probing cases and controls differently. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h3)

question: What does an odds ratio of 1.0 signify in a case-control study?

options.A: The exposure is a major protective factor against illness
options.B: The study sample size is too small to yield results
options.C: The researchers made an error in diagnostic classification
options.D: The exposure has no association with the disease

explanation: An odds ratio of 1 means the odds of exposure among cases are identical to the odds of exposure among controls. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h4)

question: In a study investigating a foodborne bacterial outbreak, the calculated odds ratio for eating contaminated egg salad is 4.5. What is the correct interpretation?

options.A: People who ate the egg salad had 4.5 times higher odds of developing the illness
options.B: There is a 4.5 percent chance that the outbreak was caused by bacteria
options.C: The controls were 4.5 times more likely to be exposed than the cases
options.D: The incidence rate of the disease in the population is exactly 4.5 percent

explanation: An odds ratio of 4.5 indicates that the exposure is strongly associated with higher odds of contracting the condition. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h4)

question: What defines a confounding variable in an epidemiological study?

options.A: An error made by the laboratory technician when reading diagnostic plates
options.B: A measurement tool that yields different values on repeated testing
options.C: A factor associated with both the exposure and the outcome, distorting the true association
options.D: A deliberate intervention introduced by the investigator to change outcomes

explanation: Confounders create a false association or mask a real one because they independently relate to both the suspected risk factor and the disease. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h5)

question: Which strategy is most effective for controlling for known confounding variables during the design phase of a case-control study?

options.A: Switching the study design from retrospective to prospective cohort
options.B: Increasing the overall sample size by a factor of ten
options.C: Matching controls to cases based on confounding characteristics like age and sex
options.D: Excluding all participants who develop symptoms during the study

explanation: Matching ensures that the case and control groups are comparable regarding potential confounders, neutralizing their distorting effect. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized advantage of a case-control study?

options.A: They can definitively establish the exact incidence rate of a disease
options.B: They require fewer study participants than large cohort studies
options.C: They are relatively inexpensive and quick to conduct
options.D: They are excellent for studying rare diseases with long latency periods

explanation: Because case-control studies start with diseased and non-diseased groups, they cannot calculate absolute disease incidence or prevalence. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h6)

question: Why is establishing a clear temporal sequence often challenging in a retrospective case-control design?

options.A: Laboratory tests take too long to process in rural health clinics
options.B: Participants change their residential addresses during the investigation
options.C: Exposure and disease status are assessed after both have already occurred
options.D: Control subjects refuse to answer questions about their medical history

explanation: Looking backward makes it difficult at times to prove conclusively whether the exposure preceded the onset of disease or resulted from early subclinical changes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of the chain of infection model in clinical practice?

options.A: To classify microorganisms according to their microscopic shape
options.B: To calculate the exact incubation period of viral pathogens
options.C: To determine the financial cost of hospital-acquired infections
options.D: To provide a framework for interrupting the transmission of pathogens

explanation: The chain of infection identifies the specific sequential steps required for a pathogen to spread, allowing healthcare workers to target interventions and break the cycle. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h1)

question: What happens to the cycle of infection if any single link in the chain is successfully removed?

options.A: Symptoms become dormant inside the host
options.B: The pathogen becomes stronger and more resistant
options.C: Transmission simply shifts to a different route
options.D: The infection cycle stops entirely

explanation: Because all six links are necessary for an infection to occur, breaking just one link halts the entire transmission process. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h1)

question: What term describes the natural habitat where an infectious agent typically lives and multiplies?

options.A: Reservoir
options.B: Portal of entry
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Vector

explanation: A reservoir provides the essential conditions for a microorganism to survive, grow, and multiply before being transferred to a new host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following represents a non-living reservoir for pathogenic microorganisms in a hospital setting?

options.A: A stray dog wandering near the ward
options.B: A patient recovering from typhoid fever
options.C: Contaminated intravenous fluid bags
options.D: An asymptomatic healthcare worker

explanation: Non-living reservoirs, also known as fomites or environmental sources, include inanimate objects like equipment, water supplies, and medications. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is a portal of exit?

options.A: The specific organ where a virus causes clinical disease
options.B: The physical barrier provided by intact human skin
options.C: The method of destroying bacteria using heat sterilization
options.D: The route through which a pathogen leaves its reservoir

explanation: The portal of exit is the specific anatomical route or bodily secretion through which a microorganism departs from the infected host or reservoir. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h3)

question: Which transmission mechanism involves pathogens being spread via tiny suspended particles that travel long distances in the air?

options.A: Airborne transmission
options.B: Vector-borne transmission
options.C: Direct contact transmission
options.D: Droplet transmission

explanation: Airborne transmission occurs when residual particles or droplet nuclei remain suspended in the air for extended periods and are inhaled by susceptible individuals. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h3)

question: What defines a susceptible host in the chain of infection?

options.A: A biological vector that carries parasites between humans
options.B: A person who actively transmits a disease without symptoms
options.C: An individual who lacks resistance to a specific pathogen
options.D: An inanimate object that harbors bacterial spores

explanation: A susceptible host is someone whose immune system cannot successfully repel an invading microorganism, allowing the pathogen to establish an infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which patient factor most directly increases overall susceptibility to nosocomial infections in a hospital ward?

options.A: Consuming a balanced hospital diet
options.B: Having normal age-appropriate vital signs
options.C: Presence of an indwelling urinary catheter
options.D: Being admitted for routine scheduled surgery

explanation: Invasive devices like urinary catheters bypass the body's natural anatomical barriers, providing a direct portal of entry and increasing infection susceptibility. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is widely recognized as the single most effective nursing action for interrupting the chain of infection?

options.A: Isolating all patients in single rooms
options.B: Performing proper hand hygiene
options.C: Changing bed linens twice daily
options.D: Administering prophylactic antibiotics

explanation: Regular and thorough hand hygiene removes transient microorganisms from the skin, preventing cross-contamination between patients and equipment. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h5)

question: A student nurse uses sterile gloves and a non-touch technique during a dressing change. Which link in the chain of infection is this intervention primarily designed to block?

options.A: Reservoir
options.B: Causative agent
options.C: Portal of entry
options.D: Portal of exit

explanation: Using sterile techniques during invasive procedures prevents pathogens from gaining access through broken skin, effectively blocking the portal of entry. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: The enforcement of hospital financial budgets and operational policies
options.B: The immediate medical treatment of individual patients in rural clinics
options.C: The systematic collection and analysis of health data to guide public health practice
options.D: The routine administration of vaccines to newborn infants

explanation: Surveillance focuses on gathering and interpreting data to plan and evaluate public health interventions rather than individual treatment. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h1)

question: Why is local clinical observation considered the foundation of national disease surveillance?

options.A: Clinical observations replace the need for laboratory confirmation of diseases
options.B: Local observations feed data upward to national agencies for early epidemic detection
options.C: Local clinics have more funding than international health organizations
options.D: Bedside nurses are solely responsible for writing national health legislation

explanation: Individual clinical observations at the facility level serve as the vital first alert for larger regional or national outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h1)

question: What justifies the mandatory reporting of infectious diseases over individual privacy rights?

options.A: The urgent need to protect public safety and prevent widespread community outbreaks
options.B: The desire of pharmaceutical companies to track drug sales and usage
options.C: The need to generate revenue through government health inspection fines
options.D: The requirement to update hospital personnel files on a monthly basis

explanation: Public health laws prioritize community safety and epidemic prevention above individual confidentiality when dealing with dangerous communicable threats. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h2)

question: Which group of professionals holds the statutory obligation to report notifiable diseases in a clinical setting?

options.A: Patient relatives and voluntary visitors
options.B: Hospital accountants and financial auditors only
options.C: Elected local government political leaders
options.D: All attending healthcare providers involved in patient care

explanation: Healthcare providers on the front lines, including nurses and doctors, bear the legal responsibility to report suspected notifiable conditions. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h2)

question: Which timeframe is generally required for reporting Category 1 epidemic-prone diseases?

options.A: Only during annual hospital accreditation
options.B: At the end of every calendar year
options.C: Within 24 hours of identification
options.D: Within 30 days of laboratory confirmation

explanation: Category 1 conditions carry high epidemic risks and demand immediate notification, usually within 24 hours, to trigger rapid containment. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h3)

question: A patient presents to a primary health clinic with acute watery diarrhea and severe dehydration during the rainy season, strongly suspected of having cholera. How should this case be classified for notification?

options.A: Non-notifiable domestic ailment
options.B: Administrative hospital incident
options.C: Category 1 immediate reportable emergency
options.D: Category 3 routine chronic condition

explanation: Cholera is a highly contagious, severe diarrheal illness classified as a Category 1 emergency requiring urgent notification. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h3)

question: Why are nurses considered the frontline of infectious disease surveillance?

options.A: They hold exclusive authority to declare national states of emergency
options.B: They conduct initial patient assessments and spend the most direct time observing clinical signs
options.C: They perform all mandatory molecular laboratory tests independently
options.D: They manage the international transport logistics for vaccines

explanation: Because nurses perform initial triage and ongoing bedside care, they are strategically positioned to spot unusual symptoms and epidemiological links first. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h4)

question: Which action is a primary responsibility of the nurse upon suspecting a highly infectious notifiable disease?

options.A: Discharging the patient immediately to avoid hospital contamination
options.B: Initiating preliminary notification and implementing isolation precautions
options.C: Destroying all clinical charts associated with the patient
options.D: Waiting for national ministers to visit before taking any action

explanation: Prompt isolation and notification are critical nursing actions to stop further pathogen transmission while awaiting formal investigation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h4)

question: What is the title of the designated officer responsible for coordinating disease surveillance at the local government level in Nigeria?

options.A: Chief Medical Director of Public Works
options.B: Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer
options.C: National Quarantine Minister
options.D: Director of Hospital Finance

explanation: The DSNO (Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer) is the specific official tasked with managing disease reports at the local government level. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the purpose of following a hierarchical reporting channel from facility to national level?

options.A: To increase paperwork burdens without adding any public health value
options.B: To deliberately delay information sharing until a disease outbreak has naturally ended
options.C: To ensure data verification, coordination, and appropriate resource mobilization at every tier
options.D: To prevent local health workers from ever communicating with federal agencies

explanation: Stepped reporting allows local validation and structured resource allocation as an outbreak moves from facility to national awareness. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary objective of contact tracing during an infectious disease outbreak?

options.A: To interview hospital administrators about facility cleaning contracts
options.B: To audit the medical insurance status of hospitalized individuals
options.C: To identify and monitor individuals exposed to an infected patient during their incubation period
options.D: To collect financial donations from family members of affected patients

explanation: Contact tracing tracks down exposed persons to monitor for early symptoms and prevent further silent community transmission. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: Why do epidemiologists plot an epidemic curve (epi-curve) during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: To visualize the timeline of cases and determine the likely pattern of transmission
options.B: To predict exact weather conditions for the upcoming planting season
options.C: To calculate the annual salary increments for hospital nursing staff
options.D: To determine the architectural layout required for new ward buildings

explanation: An epidemic curve helps investigators see whether an outbreak stems from a single common source or spreads through person-to-person contact. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: Which phase of personal protective equipment management is associated with a high risk of accidental contamination for healthcare workers?

options.A: Selecting equipment color schemes for hospital departments
options.B: Doffing (removal) of contaminated protective gear
options.C: Purchasing equipment from medical supply vendors
options.D: Storing unused gowns in clean administrative cupboards

explanation: Careless removal or doffing of PPE frequently results in infectious material transferring to the skin or scrubs of healthcare workers. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h7)

question: What is the primary difference between standard precautions and transmission-based precautions?

options.A: Standard precautions are optional guidelines, whereas transmission-based precautions carry criminal penalties
options.B: Standard precautions apply to all patient care universally, whereas transmission-based precautions target specific known or suspected pathogens
options.C: Standard precautions require full biohazard suits, while transmission-based ones require only surgical masks
options.D: Standard precautions are only used in intensive care units, while transmission-based ones are for outpatient clinics

explanation: Standard precautions form the baseline for every patient encounter, while transmission-based precautions add specific barriers for targeted routes of spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h7)

question: Which factor represents a common operational challenge in public health disease surveillance?

options.A: Underreporting by overburdened clinical personnel and poor diagnostic capacity
options.B: An excessive surplus of functional molecular testing laboratories in rural villages
options.C: Instantaneous electronic transmission of data from every household in the country
options.D: A complete absence of infectious diseases occurring within modern populations

explanation: Heavy workloads, lack of diagnostic tools, and administrative fatigue frequently lead to missed cases and delayed reporting. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h8)

question: Why is establishing feedback loops from central health authorities to frontline reporting nurses important?

options.A: It ensures that nurses receive financial bonuses for every patient admitted
options.B: It prevents regulatory bodies from inspecting clinical facilities
options.C: It maintains morale and encourages continued compliance with reporting protocols
options.D: It allows nurses to take over the ministerial duties of health directors

explanation: When frontline nurses see that their reported data leads to actionable public health interventions, they remain motivated to maintain rigorous reporting habits. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h8)

question: To which patient group do standard precautionary measures apply?

options.A: All patients receiving care regardless of diagnosis
options.B: Only patients with confirmed infectious diseases
options.C: Individuals showing visible symptoms of bleeding
options.D: Patients admitted to surgical wards exclusively

explanation: Standard precautions are universal infection control practices intended for every patient encounter, irrespective of their infection status. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h1)

question: Which bodily fluid is excluded from the application of standard precautions?

options.A: Vaginal secretions
options.B: Sweat
options.C: Saliva
options.D: Semen

explanation: Sweat is non-infectious regarding bloodborne and standard transmission routes, so it is excluded from standard precaution fluids. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h1)

question: What is the recommended duration for routine hand hygiene using an alcohol-based rub?

options.A: 20 to 30 seconds
options.B: 40 to 60 seconds
options.C: 5 to 10 seconds
options.D: 1 to 2 minutes

explanation: Alcohol-based hand rubbing requires 20 to 30 seconds of friction to effectively reduce microbial load on non-soiled hands. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h2)

question: When is soap and water handwashing strictly preferred over alcohol-based hand rub?

options.A: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids
options.B: After administering oral medications
options.C: Immediately before applying sterile gloves
options.D: When exiting a patient room without touching surfaces

explanation: Physical dirt and organic material physically shield microorganisms, requiring mechanical removal with soap and water. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of wearing a medical gown during specific clinical procedures?

options.A: To maintain a sterile surgical field for the patient
options.B: To replace the need for hand hygiene after patient contact
options.C: To keep the healthcare worker warm in cold clinical areas
options.D: To prevent soiling of clothing and protect skin from splashes

explanation: Gowns create a barrier to protect the worker's uniform and skin from contact with infectious body fluids. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h3)

question: What action should be taken immediately after removing gloves and other personal protective equipment?

options.A: Document the procedure in the chart
options.B: Perform hand hygiene
options.C: Clean the equipment for reuse
options.D: Put on a fresh pair of gloves

explanation: Microorganisms can transfer to hands during the removal of PPE, making immediate hand hygiene mandatory. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h3)

question: At what capacity level must a sharps disposal container be closed and replaced?

options.A: When it begins to smell
options.B: One-quarter full
options.C: Three-quarters full
options.D: Completely packed to the brim

explanation: Sharps containers should never be overfilled past the three-quarters mark to prevent accidental needle-sticks during disposal. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h4)

question: Why is two-handed needle recapping strictly discouraged in clinical practice?

options.A: It significantly increases the risk of accidental needle-stick injury
options.B: It wastes valuable nursing time during busy shifts
options.C: It violates medication dosage calculation standards
options.D: It damages the sharp tip, making future injections painful

explanation: Holding the cap with one hand while guiding a needle with the other frequently leads to accidental punctures of the guiding hand. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h4)

question: Where should a person direct their cough if a disposable tissue is not available?

options.A: Into the air away from people
options.B: Into the inner aspect of the elbow
options.C: Straight down toward the floor
options.D: Directly into the open palms of both hands

explanation: Coughing into the elbow prevents respiratory droplets from contaminating the hands, which frequently touch environmental surfaces. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h5)

question: A patient arrives at the outpatient clinic with a persistent cough and fever. What immediate intervention should be initiated at the entrance?

options.A: Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent transmission
options.B: Draw baseline blood cultures before allowing them to sit down
options.C: Isolate the patient in a private room for intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.D: Provide a surgical mask, tissues, and direct them to hand hygiene stations

explanation: Source control at the point of entry stops respiratory droplets from spreading in crowded waiting areas. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h5)

question: Which of the following represents a high-touch surface requiring frequent disinfection in a patient room?

options.A: The exterior window glass panes
options.B: Bed side rails and call buttons
options.C: The ceiling tiles above the bed
options.D: The upper wall corners of the room

explanation: High-touch surfaces are objects frequently contacted by patient and staff hands, making them primary vectors for cross-contamination. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of allowing a chemical disinfectant to remain wet on a surface for its specified dwell time?

options.A: To ensure sufficient contact time to destroy pathogenic microorganisms
options.B: To create a visible residue that proves the surface was cleaned
options.C: To prevent the cleaning cloth from sticking to the furniture
options.D: To neutralize harsh chemical fumes before staff enter the room

explanation: Disinfectants require a specific duration of continuous contact with pathogens to successfully break down cell walls and inactivate them. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h6)

question: Which category of healthcare waste belongs in a yellow infectious waste bag?

options.A: Soiled dressings and cotton swabs contaminated with body fluids
options.B: Used metallic needles and broken glass ampoules
options.C: Expired pharmaceutical syrups and chemical reagents
options.D: Non-hazardous office paper and food packaging waste

explanation: Yellow bags are universally designated for infectious items contaminated with blood, secretions, and excretions. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h7)

question: Why is point-of-generation waste segregation crucial in clinical wards?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any chemical disinfection of patient rooms
options.B: It prevents infectious materials from being mixed with general waste, reducing exposure risks
options.C: It reduces the financial cost of purchasing heavy-duty cleaning chemicals
options.D: It speeds up the process of making patient beds in the morning

explanation: Sorting waste right where it is generated ensures hazardous items do not accidentally contaminate non-hazardous waste streams. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h7)

question: What is the first immediate action a nurse should take after sustaining a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Squeeze the wound forcefully to express trapped blood
options.B: Wash the puncture site thoroughly with soap and running water
options.C: Apply a tight tourniquet proximal to the wound to trap blood
options.D: Report immediately to the hospital pharmacy for antibiotic drugs

explanation: Washing with soap and water is the immediate first aid step; squeezing or scrubbing can traumatize tissue and increase viral entry. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h8)

question: Why is timely reporting and evaluation critical after an occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens?

options.A: To ensure the nurse is immediately suspended from clinical duties for weeks
options.B: To fulfill legal paperwork requirements without affecting clinical health
options.C: To determine which colleague was responsible for leaving the sharp exposed
options.D: To determine source risk and initiate post-exposure prophylaxis within the optimal window

explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis for infections like HIV is most effective when administered as quickly as possible following exposure. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of a hospital Infection Control Unit?

options.A: To maintain electronic health record systems for outpatient clinics
options.B: To evaluate nursing staff performance and conduct annual salary reviews
options.C: To manage the financial budget of the hospital pharmacy department
options.D: To prevent the spread of preventable microbial pathogens in healthcare settings

explanation: The core mandate of infection control is minimizing pathogen transmission to protect patients, staff, and visitors. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h1)

question: Healthcare-acquired infections are also commonly referred to by which medical term?

options.A: Idiopathic conditions
options.B: Congenital anomalies
options.C: Nosocomial infections
options.D: Iatrogenic disorders

explanation: Nosocomial infections specifically denote illnesses originating within a hospital environment during the course of medical care. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h1)

question: Who typically serves as the operational backbone of the hospital infection control team on the wards?

options.A: The Hospital Chief Pharmacist
options.B: The Infection Control Nurse
options.C: The Chief Medical Director
options.D: The Director of Facilities

explanation: Infection Control Nurses drive daily ward-level surveillance, compliance checks, and practical staff guidance. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h2)

question: Why must the infection control unit function as a multidisciplinary team?

options.A: Medical doctors refuse to handle waste management without administrative backup
options.B: Infection prevention requires clinical, epidemiological, administrative, and environmental expertise
options.C: Microbiologists require daily assistance from pharmacists to order reagents
options.D: Hospital accreditation boards legally mandate that nurses cannot work alone

explanation: Comprehensive infection control spans patient care, data analysis, facility management, and policy enforcement, needing diverse specialists. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h2)

question: What distinguishes active surveillance from passive surveillance in hospital infection control?

options.A: Active surveillance occurs exclusively during night shifts in emergency departments
options.B: Passive surveillance utilizes advanced electronic tracking software instead of manual records
options.C: Staff actively search for infections rather than waiting for voluntary clinician reports
options.D: Active surveillance is only performed by physicians, while passive surveillance uses nurses

explanation: Active surveillance involves proactive case finding by infection control personnel to catch hidden transmission chains. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h3)

question: A hospital focuses its infection monitoring efforts strictly on the neonatal intensive care unit and surgical wards. What type of surveillance is this?

options.A: Universal surveillance
options.B: Retrospective surveillance
options.C: Targeted surveillance
options.D: Passive surveillance

explanation: Targeted surveillance concentrates resources on high-risk departments where patients are most vulnerable to severe infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary responsibility of the Infection Control Unit regarding policies?

options.A: Auditing clinical areas to ensure compliance with isolation protocols
options.B: Drafting medical malpractice legislation for the national parliament
options.C: Updating institutional guidelines on aseptic technique
options.D: Balancing international standards with local facility realities

explanation: The unit creates and enforces internal hospital policies, not national legislative laws. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h4)

question: Why must infection control policies be adapted to local infrastructural conditions within a facility?

options.A: To lower the legal liability of individual nurses during medical malpractice lawsuits
options.B: To comply with international tourism board sanitation requirements
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing imported pharmaceuticals
options.D: To ensure guidelines remain realistic and implementable despite challenges like water supply issues

explanation: Policies that ignore on-the-ground operational hurdles fail to achieve compliance from frontline clinical staff. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h4)

question: To which patient group do standard precautions apply in clinical practice?

options.A: Patients admitted exclusively to surgical and intensive care units
options.B: All patients, regardless of their diagnosis or infectious status
options.C: Individuals presenting with acute respiratory symptoms only
options.D: Only patients confirmed to have bloodborne viral infections

explanation: Standard precautions assume every patient's blood and bodily fluids are potentially infectious. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h5)

question: What is the primary rationale for conducting continuous educational workshops on personal protective equipment for hospital staff?

options.A: To evaluate nursing students for clinical grading purposes
options.B: To prevent procedural errors during the removal of contaminated gear that lead to self-contamination
options.C: To decrease the overall purchasing budget for sterile surgical gloves
options.D: To fulfill mandatory bureaucratic requirements set by insurance companies

explanation: Improper doffing of PPE frequently exposes healthcare workers to pathogens they intended to avoid. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h5)

question: What action does an Infection Control Unit take first when an unusual cluster of infections appears on a ward?

options.A: Immediately demolish and rebuild the affected ward wing
options.B: Suspend all nursing licenses across the entire hospital
options.C: Increase the price of broad-spectrum antibiotics for patients
options.D: Initiate an epidemiological investigation to define cases and trace contacts

explanation: Finding the source and scope through investigation is the critical first step before effective containment can occur. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h6)

question: What does patient cohorting mean during a hospital outbreak response?

options.A: Mixing infected and non-infected patients evenly across all available hospital beds
options.B: Discharging all vulnerable patients to isolate them at home until the outbreak clears
options.C: Grouping patients infected with the same organism together in a designated area with dedicated staff
options.D: Isolating healthcare workers in staff quarters away from all patient contact

explanation: Cohorting prevents the spread of pathogens to uninfected patients by isolating infected individuals and their caregivers together. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of color-coded waste segregation bins in a hospital setting?

options.A: To comply with interior design standards for healthcare architecture
options.B: To ensure proper separation of infectious, sharps, and general waste for safe disposal
options.C: To make the hospital corridors look more aesthetically organized for visitors
options.D: To help waste collection companies calculate their monthly recycling profits

explanation: Correct segregation prevents infectious and sharp hazards from mixing with municipal refuse, protecting workers and communities. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h7)

question: Why are high-touch surfaces in patient care areas a primary focus for the Infection Control Unit?

options.A: Hospital accreditation inspectors examine them first before checking patient charts
options.B: They collect more dust particles than ceilings and floors due to air conditioning flow
options.C: They easily harbor and transmit opportunistic pathogens between multiple hands and patients
options.D: They are the most expensive items to clean and replace in the hospital budget

explanation: Frequent hand contact transfers microorganisms to surfaces, turning them into transient reservoirs for cross-infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h7)

question: What is the main role of the Infection Control Unit regarding external public health agencies?

options.A: Serving as a liaison to report notifiable diseases and align with national health alerts
options.B: Conducting clinical drug trials for international pharmaceutical corporations
options.C: Providing financial subsidies for community health insurance schemes
options.D: Managing the political elections of local government health ministers

explanation: The unit connects internal hospital data with national disease surveillance networks to manage public health threats. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h8)

question: A patient presents to the hospital triage desk with symptoms strongly suggesting an emerging viral hemorrhagic fever. What is the immediate priority for the admitting nurse based on infection control principles?

options.A: Wait for laboratory confirmation results before applying any personal protective equipment
options.B: Transfer the patient to the general open ward to keep them comfortable
options.C: Ask the patient to return home until public health officials arrive at the clinic
options.D: Institute immediate isolation precautions and notify the hospital infection control team

explanation: Immediate barrier nursing and notification prevent wider exposure while awaiting official diagnostic confirmation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h8)

question: What term describes the biological steps through which a pathogen establishes infection and causes tissue injury?

options.A: Phagocytosis
options.B: Pathogenesis
options.C: Metaplasia
options.D: Hemostasis

explanation: Pathogenesis refers to the exact cellular and molecular mechanisms that lead to the development of a disease lesion following microbial entry. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is host tissue destruction during an infection often more severe than the direct mechanical presence of the microbe?

options.A: Normal flora reacts violently by attacking host organs directly
options.B: Red blood cells actively rupture when encountering foreign DNA
options.C: The immune response and microbial toxins contribute heavily to the damage
options.D: Pathogens consume all available oxygen in the bloodstream immediately

explanation: Much of the pathology seen in infectious lesions is collateral damage caused by the body's own inflammatory defense mechanisms alongside pathogen-derived toxins. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: What type of bacterial toxin is an integral structural component of the outer cell wall of Gram-negative organisms?

options.A: Enterotoxin
options.B: Exotoxin
options.C: Endotoxin
options.D: Neurotoxin

explanation: Endotoxins are lipopolysaccharides located within the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria that are released primarily when the cell lyses. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: How do microbial enzymes like collagenase contribute directly to the formation of a spreading tissue lesion?

options.A: By neutralizing circulating antibodies in the bloodstream
options.B: By dissolving extracellular matrix barriers to allow deeper invasion
options.C: By directly stimulating the production of protective scar tissue
options.D: By transforming normal cells into malignant neoplasms

explanation: Extracellular enzymes break down connective tissue structural proteins, stripping away barriers that would otherwise contain the localized infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which white blood cell type is the primary responder during the early acute phase of an infectious lesion?

options.A: Lymphocyte
options.B: Neutrophil
options.C: Eosinophil
options.D: Basophil

explanation: Neutrophils are recruited in massive numbers to the site of acute infection to phagocytose pathogens and release microbicidal agents. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: What defines the structural core of an abscess within an acute infectious lesion?

options.A: Proliferating fibroblasts and new blood vessels
options.B: Unaltered collagen fibers and dense scar tissue
options.C: A dormant capsule of calcified mineral deposits
options.D: Purulent exudate and liquefied cellular debris

explanation: An abscess develops when tissue undergoes liquefactive necrosis due to intense neutrophil activity, creating a pocket of pus. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which primary immune cell type characterizes chronic inflammatory lesions and granulomas?

options.A: Neutrophil
options.B: Erythrocyte
options.C: Macrophage
options.D: Platelet
